prompt: Quitanda is creating its first Redis cache on Azure today. Which service?
hint: One of the two has an announced retirement.

choices.text: Azure Cache for Redis, Premium, for clustering
choices.why: A cache that is being retired is a migration scheduled on day one.

choices.text: Azure Managed Redis, in a tier that fits the load
choices.why: Right: Microsoft names it as the service to move to.

choices.text: Azure Cache for Redis, Basic, to start cheap
choices.why: Basic has no replica and no SLA, and the service is being retired.

choices.text: A Cosmos DB container with a short time to live
choices.why: That is a database with expiry, billed in request units, not a cache in memory.

prompt: Match each Azure Cache for Redis tier to what it adds.
hint: One description belongs to Azure Managed Redis.

pairs.right: One node, no replica, no SLA
A primary and a replica, with failover

right_distractors: Tiers named Balanced and Compute Optimized

prompt: `terraform validate` accepted `sku_name = "Balanced_B1"` in `brazilsouth`. What does that prove?

choices.text: That Azure offers that size in that region
choices.why: Validate asks Azure nothing.

choices.text: That the cache will be clustered with the OSS policy
choices.why: That is a different line, and also only checked against a list.

choices.text: Only that the name is in the provider's list
choices.why: Right: the same list it printed for a wrong eviction policy.

choices.text: That the cache has a replica of every shard
choices.why: `high_availability_enabled` declares that; nothing created it.

prompt: A program connects to an Azure Cache for Redis on port 6379 and is refused. What is the likely reason?

choices.text: The cache is full and refuses new connections
choices.why: A full cache refuses writes, not connections.

choices.text: The plain-text port is off by default; TLS is on 6380
choices.why: Right: connect on 6380 with TLS.

choices.text: `CONFIG` is blocked, so the client cannot negotiate
choices.why: Clients do not need `CONFIG` to connect.

choices.text: Basic caches accept no connections from outside Azure
choices.why: The tier does not decide this; the port does.

prompt: The local Redis reported `maxmemory` 0 and `noeviction`. What happens when it runs out of memory?

choices.text: It evicts the least recently used keys
choices.why: That is `allkeys-lru`.

choices.text: It writes the oldest keys to disk
choices.why: Redis does not page keys out; persistence is a separate feature.

choices.text: It refuses writes
choices.why: Right, once the machine's memory is used; 0 means no limit of its own.

choices.text: It restarts empty
choices.why: Nothing restarts; writes are refused with an error.

prompt: Why can you not check a managed cache's eviction policy the way this section did?
hint: Which command did the section use?

choices.text: The service blocks `CONFIG` on its caches
choices.why: Right: the settings belong to the service; read them from its configuration.

choices.text: Managed caches have no eviction policy
choices.why: They have one; Azure Cache for Redis's default is `volatile-lru`.

choices.text: `redis-cli` cannot reach a cache outside Docker
choices.why: It can, with the address, the port and TLS.

choices.text: The policy is only visible in the Azure invoice
choices.why: It is a setting of the cache, not a billing line.

prompt: Which of these does the local Redis container teach you about Azure's services? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: How a key with a time to live expires
choices.why: Right: the engine's behaviour.

choices.text: Which keys each eviction policy throws away
choices.why: Right: also the engine's.

choices.text: How long failover to a replica takes
choices.why: There is no replica here; that is the service.

choices.text: What a cache of a given size costs a month
choices.why: Prices come from the price sheet, not from a container.

prompt: Put in order what `product()` in `cache.py` does on a miss.
items: `GET product:cafe-500g` from Redis, which answers nothing
Read the item from Cosmos DB
Return it, saying it came from the database

prompt: After the first price change, what price in reais did the page show?
Why does a write delete the cached key rather than write the new value into it?

choices.text: Redis cannot overwrite a key that has a time to live
choices.why: It can; `SET` replaces the key and its expiry.

choices.text: Deleting is cheaper in request units
choices.why: Redis does not bill in request units.

choices.text: Racing writers leave stale values; a delete costs one miss
choices.why: Right: the next reader refills it from Cosmos DB.

choices.text: The time to live would be reset to zero
choices.why: A `SET` with `EX` sets a fresh one.

prompt: Every write now deletes its key. Why keep the 300-second time to live at all?
hint: What if the delete never happens?

choices.text: Redis refuses keys with no expiry
choices.why: It accepts them, and `volatile-lru` would then never evict them.

choices.text: A failed delete leaves a stale copy behind
choices.why: Right, and under `volatile-lru` it also makes the key evictable.

choices.text: So that popular keys never miss
choices.why: Expiry causes misses, it does not prevent them.

choices.text: Cosmos DB requires its readers to cache for at most five minutes
choices.why: No such rule exists.

prompt: With `volatile-lru` and no time to live on any key, how many of the 10,000 writes did `fill.py` get refused?
Quitanda's catalogue cache holds only copies of Cosmos DB items, some written without a time to live. Which policy?

choices.text: `noeviction`, so nothing is lost
choices.why: Nothing in it is lost if evicted; the database has it. Refusing writes is the failure.

choices.text: `volatile-lru`, Azure Cache for Redis's default
choices.why: Keys without a time to live could never be evicted, and the cache would fill and refuse.

choices.text: `allkeys-lru`, evicting the least recently read
choices.why: Right: any copy may go, the least recently read first.

choices.text: `volatile-ttl`, to evict whatever expires soonest
choices.why: Still only keys with a time to live.

prompt: A policy whose name starts with `volatile-` may evict only keys that have a time to ___.
hint: The English phrase the Portuguese keeps.

prompt: `allkeys-lru` reported 2,955 keys kept in one run and a few different in another. Why?
hint: How does Redis pick a key to evict?

choices.text: Some writes were lost on the network
choices.why: Every write was answered; none was refused.

choices.text: It samples candidates rather than searching every key
choices.why: Right: an approximation of least recently used, so counts move a little.

choices.text: The 4 MB limit is enforced only once a second
choices.why: It is checked as writes arrive.

choices.text: Keys with the same value are stored once
choices.why: Redis does not deduplicate values.

prompt: How many hash slots does a Redis cluster divide its keys into?
`MSET` of the two products was refused with `CROSSSLOT` on a one-node cluster. Why, when both slots were on the same machine?

choices.text: The rule is about slots, so it holds however slots are placed
choices.why: Right: 8271 and 5910 are two slots, and code must not depend on where they live.

choices.text: The node had not finished taking the slots
choices.why: It answered the cart keys' `MSET` with OK a moment later.

choices.text: `MSET` is not allowed on a cluster at all
choices.why: It is, for keys in one slot.

choices.text: Product keys need the OSS policy
choices.why: Policies belong to Azure Managed Redis; this was the engine.

prompt: In `{cart:c-7}:items`, only the part inside the braces is hashed. That part is called a hash ___.
hint: It labels which keys go together.

prompt: A developer puts every key of the shop under the hash tag `{quitanda}` so that any `MSET` works. What goes wrong?
hint: Where do all those keys live?

choices.text: Redis refuses a hash tag used by more than one key
choices.why: Sharing is the point of a tag.

choices.text: The keys are spread at random instead
choices.why: They all hash to one slot.

choices.text: Every key lands on one shard, a hot partition
choices.why: Right: one slot, one shard, and the rest of the cluster idle.

choices.text: `CROSSSLOT` errors become more frequent
choices.why: They disappear, which is why it is tempting.

prompt: Under Azure Managed Redis's Enterprise clustering policy, how does a client see the shards?

choices.text: It connects to each shard and computes slots itself
choices.why: That is the OSS policy.

choices.text: Through one endpoint, and the service routes
choices.why: Right: a client written for one server connects unchanged.

choices.text: It does not: Enterprise caches have one shard
choices.why: Azure Managed Redis is always sharded.

choices.text: Through the hash tags it declares in advance
choices.why: Tags are in key names; nothing is declared.

prompt: Which of these say the catalogue cache is being used as more than a cache? Choose all that apply.
hint: Could it be emptied tonight without loss?

choices.text: Persistence was switched on so that a restart is not empty
choices.why: Right: a pure cache refills from Cosmos DB.

choices.text: Some values exist only in Redis
choices.why: Right: then it is the database.

choices.text: The policy is `noeviction` so that nothing is ever dropped
choices.why: Right: a cache that must not forget is not a cache.

choices.text: Keys are written with a 300-second time to live
choices.why: That is ordinary cache-aside.

prompt: Quitanda's cart keeps `{cart:c-7}:items` and `{cart:c-7}:total` and updates both in one transaction. Why the braces?

choices.text: Braces make a key expire with its neighbours
choices.why: Expiry is per key.

choices.text: They encrypt the customer id
choices.why: They change only what is hashed.

choices.text: Both names hash to one slot
choices.why: Right: commands over several keys need one slot.

choices.text: Redis requires braces in every key name on a cluster
choices.why: They are optional, and the product keys had none.
